Current law is the law in force on the as-of date. A rule enacted on or before the as-of date with a later effective date is current law from its effective date: when that date falls inside 2027-2031 it is modelled as a reform with a start delay equal to the years between January 1, 2027 and the effective date (the reform's start_delay_years entry), and the run names it. Bills not enacted by the as-of date are scenarios, never baseline. The benchmark reforms are assumed in force on January 1, 2027.

Interest rates, construction costs, rents, home values and household incomes are held at the levels in the ledger and the data packs for the whole window (2027-2031). The baseline repeats recent permit trends under today's rules; it does not predict a recession or a boom. Only the ranges of the ledger entries and the baseline's back-tested range carry uncertainty about them.

New privately owned housing units authorized by building permits, as the Census Bureau's Building Permits Survey counts them, in the five calendar years 2027-2031. A reform's number is the difference from the baseline in the same unit: permits the reform adds, less permits the baseline would have issued anyway on the same sites. The Building Permits Survey leaves out additions, alterations, renovations and conversions of existing buildings, so a unit created that way is not in this measure.

Added units authorized count every new unit that needs a permit. Net added homes subtract the existing homes a project demolishes (the reform's share of them: a demolition that would have happened in the baseline anyway is not the reform's). One house replaced by three homes is three authorizations and two more homes.

What these estimates cannot tell you
These are ranges of building permits, not a forecast of homes finished.
A reform's likely range is a simulation range: it shows how the result moves with the assumptions, given the baseline. No reform of this kind has past totals to check it against.
They describe the whole state. They do not say which lots, streets or owners would build.
They do not say who would live in the new homes or what they would pay.
They assume every town follows the new rule from the first day and approves permits at today's pace.
They say nothing about years after the five-year period.
The baseline repeats recent permit trends under today's rules. It does not predict a recession or a boom.

The baseline range is not a promise. Tested on past years, using only what was known at the time, ranges built this way caught the real five-year total less often than eight times in ten for counties. Each range states how often ranges like it caught the real total.
Those past years hold about one housing cycle, and misses ran mostly to one side and moved together across counties, so the share caught rests on few independent periods.

The rule behind the range was chosen using every past year, including the years it was later scored on, and with today's county types rather than those known at the time, so the share caught is somewhat favourable. Each count's validation card names the study, years and area it comes from.

In every draw all counties sit at the same point of the housing cycle, and costs, credit and review speed are drawn on their own. A separate sensitivity shows the ranges when regions swing apart inside the state range and when high costs, tight credit and slow review come together; it does not replace these ranges.
Counties without a permit office, or with imputed permit counts, carry the Census Bureau's estimates.

The year between the last full year of permit data and the first projected year has no full-year count yet. The baseline carries the latest yearly level through it; a nowcast from the monthly files is shown as a check only, and a part-year count is never treated as a full year.

The middle value depends on which past years the rule averages. In Pennsylvania one unusually high year sits in the window; the baseline card shows the effect of leaving it out as a disclosed sensitivity, not a replacement.

In states with a short permit record, the range is widened toward the past errors of states that grew at a similar pace. Those errors come from one recovery after a housing bust, so the next cycle may differ, and the ranges still caught the real total less often than they aim to.

Where the baseline itself has been least accurate in past years: 'Rural, slow-growth, lower-cost' counties (where it has tended to run too high) and small counties (where it has tended to run too high). Read the change in those places with extra care; the Method page shows the back-test.
Whether an ADU fits on a given lot: the fit test is a share for each census tract, not a site plan.
Septic limits, steep slopes, flood zones, historic districts and private deed rules, none of which are in the fit test.
Whether towns slow approvals or add new hurdles.
How quickly owners take up the new right. This is the widest assumption and is not yet checked against places like this state.

Whether every ADU shows up in permit statistics. Many towns permit an ADU as an addition or a conversion, not as a new home, and the national permit survey does not count those, so some of the homes added here may never appear in published permit counts.

State reform law on the five reforms
Text read 2026-11-24 (statutes as compiled after the 2026 budget session)
No provision listed for this state has a dated record of enactment or effect; the statutes listed leave these rules to local codes.
W.S. 15-1-601 and 18-5-201 (no accessory dwelling unit section) (accessory dwelling units)
enacted; in force on 2026-11-24: not known (no dated record)

Wyoming's zoning statutes do not mention accessory dwelling units. Whether one may be added to a single-family lot is left to each city, town and county zoning code. Against the benchmark: The whole benchmark is new at state level: no lot is opened to an ADU by state law. The share already legal comes from local codes, which are not read for Wyoming, so the national default range is used.
W.S. 15-1-601 (city and town zoning powers) (missing-middle housing)

A city or town may regulate building height, size, lot coverage, yards, population density and land use, by districts, uniform within each district, in line with a comprehensive plan. The statute permits local rules; it does not require any district to allow more than one home. Against the benchmark: No state rule allows two to six homes on single-family lots; the benchmark would be new everywhere it applies.

If owners of 20% or more of the land in a proposed zoning change, or within 140 feet of it, protest, the change needs three-quarters of the whole city or town council. Bills to repeal or amend this failed in 2026. Against the benchmark: A higher bar for town-by-town upzoning; it does not apply to a state reform. Shown as context for how slowly local rules change without one.
W.S. 18-5-201 with 18-5-303(a)(i) (county zoning; family land divisions) (missing-middle housing)

A county may zone its unincorporated land, but may not use a minimum lot size or other rule to stop a home or farm use on a land division that is exempt from subdivision review because it is a single gift or sale to an immediate family member. Against the benchmark: Narrow: it protects one home on a family land division, not more homes on an existing lot.
Wyoming statutes (no residential parking-minimum or development impact fee section) (development fees)

No Wyoming statute sets, caps or forbids residential parking minimums, and none sets a framework for development impact fees; both are local choices where they exist. Against the benchmark: The parking and fee benchmarks would be new at state level.

Screening measures only: they show where building may be harder, not what the rules allow, and they do not change the model's estimates. The flood share uses FEMA's regulatory 1% annual chance floodplain; it leaves out heavy-rain flooding away from mapped streams, and some flood maps are decades old. Where FEMA has no digital map the flood shares are blank, not zero. A home counts as in the floodplain when its 2020 Census block's centre point falls on a 30 m grid cell inside the floodplain, so large rural blocks are coarse. Land cover is a 30 m satellite classification; developed land includes parks and lawns. Slope comes from a 30 m elevation grid, which smooths short steep banks, so the steep share is a lower bound for small sites.

The report card describes the whole state's data, not this place alone. Taken from the Assumption Ledger, not state data: Share of residential land zoned for single-family homes only; Share of lots where an ADU is already allowed; Share of lots with room for a detached ADU (needs parcels); Development and impact fees per unit; Parking spaces required per unit.
American Community Survey 5-year table-based summary files (2020-2024)

Estimates are survey averages over five years with margins of error; small tracts often have wide margins. One national pipe-delimited file per table (about 48 MB for B25024). Negative values are missing-value codes, not data.
American Community Survey 5-year tables for the place-profile charts (2020-2024)

Survey estimates averaged over five years, with margins of error; tract counts in small bands are often very uncertain. Bands are sums of published cells; a band's margin is the Bureau's approximation for a sum. To keep the pack small, tracts keep only age, race and ethnicity, household income, commute mode and rent burden (counties and the state keep every table).
FHFA House Price Index, annual, counties

Repeat-sales index built from mortgages bought or guaranteed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac; thin in rural counties, where years can be missing. Published as a spreadsheet (read with the standard library's zip and XML tools).
LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES 8), workplace area characteristics, all jobs
U.S. Census Bureau, Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics program

Counts jobs covered by unemployment insurance plus federal civilian jobs, by where people work. Self-employed people, the military and informal work are not counted. A person with two jobs counts twice. The Census Bureau adds noise to block counts for privacy; tract and county sums are much steadier.
LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LODES 8), home-to-work flows, all jobs

Links each job's workplace block to the worker's home block. The "main" file covers jobs with both ends in the state; the "aux" file adds workers who live in another state. Residents who work in another state are in that state's files, which are not read, so out-commuting across the state line is not counted. Same job coverage as the workplace file.

Counts private establishments with paid employees and their mid-March employment and yearly payroll. Government, self-employed and most farm work are left out. Small cells carry noise; the noise flag is kept. Establishments that cannot be placed in a county are left out, so counties do not add up to the state total.
Building Permits Survey, county annual files
Counts units authorized by permit, not units started or finished. Some counties are imputed rather than reported; the file flags which. Places without permit offices are not covered.
Comprehensive Housing Affordability Strategy (CHAS) data, Tables 8, 12 and 15C
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Policy Development and Research (special tabulation of ACS data by the Census Bureau)

Survey estimates averaged over five years, rounded by the Census Bureau, with margins of error; small tract cells are very uncertain. Income bands are shares of HUD area median family income (HAMFI) for the household's area, not of a county's own median. Cost burden is housing costs (gross rent, or owner costs) over household income; households with no or negative income are "not computed". The edition is older than the ACS 2020-2024 tables used elsewhere.
HUD income limits (Section 8), area median family income and 30%, 50% and 80% limits by household size
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Policy Development and Research

Limits are set per HUD area (a metro area or a non-metro county) with caps, floors and state non-metro adjustments, so the 80% limit is not always 1.6 times the 50% limit and the 30% limit can be raised to the poverty guideline. The 60% and 100% figures used for rents are derived from the 50% limit (x1.2 and x2), the convention HUD uses for tax-credit limits; they are not published here.
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD eGIS open data)

Properties with an active HUD project-based assistance contract (Section 8, Section 202/811 and similar). Only the first two contracts of a property carry units and an expiration date; a third or later contract is not dated here. Many contracts are renewed when they expire, so "expiring" marks a renewal decision, not a certain loss. Properties that also hold tax credits are counted in both programs.

Public housing developments as reported by housing agencies; a scattered-site development is one point. Units converted to project-based contracts (RAD) leave this list and appear among assisted multifamily properties.
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit properties (HUD LIHTC database)
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development

Projects placed in service since 1987 as reported by state agencies; recent years are incomplete (the map service's Pennsylvania records stop at 2020) and the year is unknown for some projects. A project's point is the address of its largest building. Projects that left the program are not removed.
HUD Housing Choice Vouchers by Tract (map service)

Households using a tenant-based voucher, by the tract of the home they rent. Vouchers move with the household, so they are assisted households, not assisted homes, and are kept apart from the unit counts. Small counts are suppressed by HUD.
Wyoming Statutes Titles 15 and 18 (city, town and county zoning) and session bill digests

The statutes say what cities, towns and counties may regulate, not what each local code allows today. Wyoming has no state ADU, missing-middle, transit-density, parking or fee statute, so this source supports a finding of silence, not a share of lots. The web PDFs are unofficial compilations.
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit Qualified Census Tracts

A Qualified Census Tract lets a tax-credit project claim a 30% larger basis. Designations change every year; HUD's map item and layer text name different years (2026 and 2027), so the edition is stated as published. Being in a QCT does not mean a project will get credits.
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit Difficult Development Areas

In metro areas, Difficult Development Areas are ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs); outside them, whole counties. A tract is matched to ZCTAs by shared land area, so a tract on a ZCTA edge can be partly in a DDA.
Qualified Opportunity Zones designated for 2027 (second decennial round)

The new round of zones starts on 2027-01-01. The first-round zones (2018, on 2010 tracts) end on 2026-12-31 and are not shown. Treasury says taxpayers may not rely on the web list to support a tax position.
New Markets Tax Credit low-income community tracts (2016-2020 ACS)
U.S. Department of the Treasury, CDFI Fund

Shows whether a tract meets the poverty (20% or more) or income (80% of the benchmark or less) test. Other routes to eligibility (high-migration rural counties, targeted populations) are not shown. The CDFI Fund does not update the file every year.
National Register of Historic Places, listed property points and polygons
U.S. Department of the Interior, National Park Service

Only properties NPS has mapped and does not restrict are shown, so counts are a floor. A district polygon's homes are 2020 Census block homes whose block centre is inside it. Listing makes income-producing rehabilitation eligible for the federal historic tax credit; it does not grant one.
U.S. Department of Transportation, Bureau of Transportation Statistics

Stops as reported by agencies in their schedule feeds; some agencies are missing or out of date. Gives stop locations, not service frequency (frequency comes from the agency schedule feeds). About 673,000 stops nationally; queried by state bounding box in pages of at most 2,000.

Housing units and population are 2020 counts, not current. Internal points are a point inside each block, not its centre of population. Only the attribute table (the .dbf, about 46 MB of the 409 MB Pennsylvania zip) is read, by HTTP range requests; block shapes are never downloaded.
EPA sewersheds of the United States (version 1.3) and their endpoint treatment plants
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Office of Research and Development, Office of Water)

Context only. Most boundaries are modelled with machine learning from hexagons of about 0.11 square km (Pennsylvania: 799 of 838 modelled; Vermont: 92 of 93 taken from a 2009 state map); EPA says they are not an authoritative source for property-level connections. Never used for a tract's sewer status.
EPA Clean Watersheds Needs Survey 2022, documented needs by county
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Office of Water)

Capital needs states documented for the survey (projects eligible for Clean Water State Revolving Fund loans), summarized by county by EPA. Context only: a large need is not a shortage of capacity, and a zero can mean nothing was submitted.
FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (flood hazard zones and NFHL availability), public map service

The Special Flood Hazard Area is the regulatory 1% annual chance floodplain; it leaves out flooding from heavy rain away from mapped streams, and some maps are decades old. Where FEMA has no digital map (outside layer 0, "NFHL availability") flood shares are left blank rather than zero.
USGS Annual NLCD land cover and fractional impervious surface (Collection 1), MRLC coverage service
U.S. Geological Survey (Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium)
Satellite classification at 30 m: small lots, narrow streets and tree-covered yards are blurred; the developed classes include parks and lawns (class 21). Screening only.
USGS 3D Elevation Program bare-earth elevation (3DEPElevation image service)
Resampled by the service to 30 m (bilinear), so short steep banks are smoothed and the steep share is a lower bound for small sites. Screening only.
Generalized (simplified) shapes for maps, not for measuring land area or for parcel work. 2020 tracts match the 2020-2024 ACS.
Transit agency schedule feeds (GTFS), via their published addresses or the catalog mirror
Each transit agency (copies mirrored by MobilityData)

Scheduled, not actual, service. One representative weekday per feed. Only feeds that download without a key are used; bus stops of other agencies are marked frequency unknown. Agencies change stop ids between schedules, so a few stops may not match the National Transit Map.
Primary Mortgage Market Survey, weekly rate history
National average offered rates for prime borrowers, not the rate a given household or builder pays. The value used in the model is a ledger parameter with a range.
Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, annual averages, construction (NAICS 23)

Average pay of construction jobs at private employers, by where the employer reports, not where it builds. A wage index is a proxy for local building costs; materials, land and fees are not in it. BLS withholds county figures that would reveal one employer; those counties take the state value.

The top driver of each reform is worked out for the whole state, not for the district.
